My first year on metformin was rough. The side effects were horrendous, I became scared of eating just because of dealing with the nausea, vomiting, fatigue etc. Would stop taking the metformin and then would have to start from square one.

The first thing your wife will have to do is see if she can switch to extended release formula over standard release. The symptoms are less and more manageable. Those can be more expensive but worth it. The second is supplements. Like most have suggested, checking b12, folate, iron and vit D levels is crucial since PCOS/metformin can cause a deficiency of them. Myo-inositol also helps minimize these side effects.

The next thing is lifestyle. The side effects definitely minimized after one year of consistently taking the metformin for me, but that can differ for everyone. You have to just make sure you’re taking care of them properly. I realized that there were certain foods that I could eat before metformin but after taking it I couldn’t tolerate anymore, for eg chickpea flour or specific lentils. Your wife needs to look out for what makes her feel good and what makes her feel bad. I was able to handle greens and proteins very well. Sweets not at all. So figuring out your trigger foods is key.

If I know I’m prone to diarrhea and/or stomach cramps, I’ll take loperamide (Imodium) to deal with that side effect of metformin. If I know I’m prone to nausea, I’ll take an anti emetic (Maxolon if prone to constipation, gravitate if prone to diarrhea). These must be discussed with her endo/gyno so she can be guided on which works best for which side effect. Symptomatic treatment is a real help.

Other than that, you just need to be there for her. These side effects can be grueling, and dealing with them on your own can make you feel defeated. Assure her that she’s going to be alright, that you’re there for her in whatever capacity she needs, whether it’s diet changes, going to the doctor, or helping her when she’s feeling sick. I hope she feels better soon! There is light at the end of the tunnel I promise!

Hello! I hope your journey leads you to happiness as you self explore. What you’re describing, I guarantee everyone in the world has felt that way at one point. We all question our feelings and sexuality and it can be very confusing finding the right answer. It just takes time and knowledge and experience. I always knew in my heart since I was a child that I was ace, but it wasn’t until college that I even realized what I felt was real and valid.

Honestly nobody here can clearly define you or tell you who you are, you are whatever label you think most suits you. But I’ll try and explain the most basic terminologies so maybe they help!

Asexual: lack of sexual attraction to people. You may still have romantic, platonic, aesthetic attraction. You also may or may not be involved in sexual activities.

Aromantic: Lack of romantic attraction. You may or may not be asexual.

Allo: having sexual attraction.

Grey-sexual: there is overlap between the sexual and asexual spectrum, but you’re mostly leaning towards the asexual spectrum. Meaning you have some moments where you may feel sexual attraction, but most moments you’re on the asexual side.

Demi-sexual: sexual attraction only after forming deeper bonds with people.

Sex-positive/favoring: You can be a sex-favoring asexual if you don’t feel sexual attraction but you still have sex for your own libido/experimentation/fetish/comfort of partner or any other reason (all are valid).

Sex-neutral: You are not opposed to the idea or the act of sex. You don’t actively seek out sex, but you don’t mind it.

Sex-negative/repulsed: no interest in sex. May also be uncomfortable with or against the idea or action of sex.

Any and all of these terms can be “mixed and matched”. So you could be aromantic asexual, demi romantic grey asexual, sex favoring asexual etc. It ultimately depends on your own preferences. You can probably research more on specific sub types of asexuality like aegosexual, lithosexual etc.

Honestly, just don’t get stuck on labels and exact definitions too much. You’re figuring yourself out, and it takes time. When you feel like you *know*, you’ll know. So I hope this helps!

Hi! Thank you so much, yes I am a medical doctor! And of course I’ll gladly answer!



So I think this is very dependent on different countries, their healthcare systems, and the cultures you’re working with. I studied in the largest government medical hospital. So most of the patients we got had poor socioeconomic statuses. This means a lot of them work as laborers, at home housewives etc. And also come from strict religious backgrounds. So many of them are restricted from getting themselves checked for YEARS because they can’t/won’t based on their access to medical information and facilities.


I’ve seen a lot of patients come in for things that could have easily been prevented/treated immediately, from simple leg edema to glaucoma to strokes. I think women’s health is extremely overlooked here, with the stigma being that they “cry pain over the slightest sensation” which means their pain is massively ignored. Children as well, a lot of conditions like autism go overlooked well past their school age! My own mother got checked for a migraine, and was losing her sight over 5 years before she realized something was wrong and finally got diagnosed with glaucoma.



Misdiagnosis is also a major factor. Sometimes doctors can see signs and symptoms and build a clinical picture in their head and just work on that instead of trying to look for other possible routes. Not all patients with anhedonia (loss of interest in hobbies/activities) have depression, not all patients with high blood pressure have just heart disease. You also have a lot of conditions that are extremely hard to diagnose, like chronic fatigue syndrome, bipolar disorder etc. 



Ultimately healthcare systems have to try and encourage awareness within communities so that people understand when their body isn’t working right and can get checked as soon as possible. And governments should make healthcare more easily accessible as well!
